planting.note: Wait until soil has warmed past 65F, since this South African heirloom is notably frost-sensitive even by pumpkin standards.

directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills spaced widely apart once soil is reliably warm, as this variety resents any lingering chill. Vines are vigorous and sprawling, so give them ample room or train them along a fence. The flattened, pale ivory fruit develops slight ribbing and deep orange flesh as it matures, and it is ready to harvest once the rind resists a thumbnail. Cure fruit in a warm spot for one to two weeks before moving to cool storage, where the flat shape makes stacking easy through winter.
sources: Slow Food Foundation Ark of Taste

planting.note: Direct sow after danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed, since moschata types are slow to establish in cool ground.

directions: One of the oldest documented American pumpkin varieties, dating to before 1824, this heirloom produces a flattened, wheel-of-cheese shaped fruit with smooth tan skin and moderate ribbing. Sow directly in hills after the soil warms, allowing plenty of room for the sprawling vines. Fruit is ready when the rind hardens and takes on a uniform tan color; harvest with several inches of stem attached. The deep orange flesh is dense, sweet, and stores exceptionally well through winter, making it a reliable keeper for pies and baking.

planting.note: Direct sow once soil is consistently warm; can also be started indoors 2-3 weeks early in short-season regions and transplanted carefully to avoid root disturbance.

directions: A traditional Japanese kabocha type especially popular around Tokyo, prized for its dry, deep-yellow, chestnut-flavored flesh. Sow directly after frost danger passes, or start indoors for an earlier crop in cool climates. Vines set three to four uniform, squat globe-shaped fruits with dark green skin and faint white speckling. Harvest once the skin dulls and resists puncture, then cure in a warm location for a week or two; curing converts starches to sugars and noticeably improves flavor. Stores well for several months in a cool, dry spot.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost; this drought-tolerant heirloom from Idaho river country adapts well to short, dry growing seasons.

directions: A rare Pacific Northwest heirloom preserved by home gardeners along the Lower Salmon River in Idaho and later distributed through Slow Food Ark of Taste seed-saving networks. Sow directly in hills after frost danger passes; the vines are relatively compact and early-maturing compared to many winter squash. Fruits are round with peach-to-orange skin, occasionally showing faint turban shaping, and average five to seven pounds. Harvest when the rind is hard and stem has begun to dry, then cure briefly before storing; the thick skin resists rot and rodent damage, allowing fruit to keep for many months.
sources: Slow Food USA Ark of Taste

planting.note: Direct sow once soil has warmed after last frost; give vines a long, frost-free season to reach full size.

directions: Developed in the late 1940s as a cross between Blue Hubbard and Sweet Meat squash, this heirloom keeps the rich, sweet flesh of its parents in a more manageable, thinner-shelled fruit. Sow directly in well-amended hills spaced widely apart, since vines are vigorous and long-running. Fruits have blue-gray, lightly warted skin and grow to fifteen pounds or more. Harvest before the first hard freeze once the rind is fully hardened, cure for a week in a warm room, and store in a cool, dry location, where it will keep for months longer than standard Blue Hubbard.
sources: Slow Food USA Ark of Taste

planting.note: Direct sow in hills after last frost, traditionally planted alongside corn and beans in a Three Sisters arrangement.

directions: A traditional squash of the Hidatsa people of the upper Missouri River valley in present-day North Dakota, grown for generations as part of the Three Sisters companion planting system with corn and beans. Sow seeds directly in hills after frost danger passes; the vigorous vines are notably drought tolerant, reflecting their origin on the Northern Plains. Fruit is teardrop-shaped with salmon-pink skin and thick, deep orange flesh, typically ten to twenty inches long. Harvest once the rind hardens and resists puncture, then store in a cool, dry place, where its excellent keeping quality made it a reliable winter food source.
